stats.label: people live with a rare disease

statsHover:
CDG (Congenital Disorders of Glycosylation) is not one disease but a large group of rare genetic metabolic disorders. More than 160 genes (about 170) are known whose mutations cause different forms of CDG, and this number keeps growing as new genes are discovered.

The best-known and most common type is PMM2-CDG (formerly CDG-Ia or Jaeken syndrome). It was the first clinically described form, is still the most frequent, and accounts for about 60% of all CDG cases.

Latest data: worldwide, about 1 in 127 people is autistic (WHO, 2025); in the US, 1 in 31 children (CDC); in Georgia, 4.25% (about 1 in 24–25 children) (2025–2026 study). The rise in these numbers is mainly linked to better diagnosis and greater awareness.

More than 300 million people worldwide live with one of over 6,000 known rare diseases, most of which have a genetic basis. About 70% of rare diseases begin in childhood, and about half of patients are children. That is why early diagnosis, accurate information, specialist involvement and family support play a decisive role.

cdg.title: What is CDG?
cdg.text: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) are a large group of rare genetic conditions. They affect how the body attaches sugar chains (glycans) to proteins and fats — a process almost every cell depends on. Because of this, CDG can affect many organs at once: the brain, muscles, liver, eyes and heart.

autism.eyebrow: A different way of experiencing the world
autism.title: What is autism?
autism.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that shapes how a person communicates, interacts with others and experiences the world. It is a spectrum: every autistic person has their own strengths and needs, and early, individual support makes a real difference.

cdg.title: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG)
cdg.lead: CDG is a family of more than 160 rare, inherited metabolic conditions. Most children are diagnosed in infancy, and symptoms can range from mild to severe.

sections.title: What is CDG?
paragraphs: Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) are a large group of rare genetic disorders that affect glycosylation — the process of adding sugar building blocks, called glycans, to proteins and fats in cells throughout the body.

Glycans help proteins fold correctly, travel to the right place and do their job. When glycosylation does not work properly, many body systems can be affected at the same time. CDG is not related to diabetes, even though it involves sugars.
The most common type is PMM2-CDG (formerly called CDG-Ia). Each type is named after the gene that causes it.

sections.title: Causes
paragraphs: CDG is caused by changes (variants) in genes that control glycosylation. More than 400 genes take part in this process, and changes in more than 160 of them (about 170) are a known cause of CDG.

Most types are inherited in an autosomal recessive way: a child becomes affected when they receive the changed copy of the gene from both parents. The parents are usually healthy carriers. When both parents are carriers, the chance of the disease in each pregnancy is 25% (a 50% chance the child is a carrier, and a 25% chance they do not have the change at all).
A few types are inherited differently (autosomal dominant or X-linked), and some result from a new (de novo) change in the child's gene, meaning the parents do not have the same change.

sections.title: Signs and symptoms
paragraphs: Symptoms vary widely between types of CDG, and sometimes even between children with the same type. They often appear in infancy and may include:
list: Low muscle tone (hypotonia) and developmental delay
Feeding difficulties and poor growth
Squint (strabismus) and vision problems
Unusual distribution of fat tissue, sunken nipples or other physical features
Liver problems and blood clotting disorders
Seizures and stroke-like episodes
Balance and coordination problems (ataxia)
Heart, kidney or hormonal problems
sections.after: In older children and adults, balance, speech, puberty, scoliosis (curvature of the spine), joint stiffness and vision difficulties may become more noticeable.

sections.title: Diagnosis
paragraphs: Because CDG is rare and its symptoms overlap with other conditions, diagnosis can take time. A doctor may suspect CDG when a child has problems in several body systems at once.

A blood test, transferrin glycosylation analysis (isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry), often reveals abnormal glycans. However, a standard blood test is not enough in every case, and sometimes the result can be normal.

The exact type of CDG is confirmed by genetic testing: a gene panel, exome or genome sequencing. When the specific genetic variant in a family is already known, genetic counselling helps parents understand the risks and options for future pregnancies. In the case of autosomal recessive inheritance, when both parents are carriers, the chance of CDG in each subsequent child is 25%.

sections.title: Treatment and care
paragraphs: For most types of CDG there is no cure yet, so care focuses on managing symptoms and supporting development. A team of specialists usually works together:
list: A neurologist, geneticist and metabolic disease specialist
Nutritional support, including a feeding tube when needed
Physical, occupational and speech therapy
Anti-seizure medication when needed
Regular monitoring of the liver, blood clotting, heart and hormones
Eye care, glasses and orthopaedic support
sections.after: For some types, direct treatment is possible: for example, MPI-CDG responds well to oral mannose, and some other types are helped by specific sugar supplements. Research into new therapies is actively continuing around the world, and it is equally important that families stay informed and receive emotional support.

sections.title: Outlook
paragraphs: The outlook depends significantly on the specific type of CDG and its severity. Some children have relatively mild symptoms, while others need lifelong care, specialist involvement and regular monitoring.
Thanks to early diagnosis, coordinated medical care, therapy, family support and an understanding society, many children with CDG develop steadily and live full, dignified lives.

autism.title: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
autism.lead: Autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition. It is not an illness to be cured, but a different way of thinking, communicating and experiencing the world — one that deserves understanding and the right support.

sections.title: What is autism?
paragraphs: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects how a person communicates and interacts with others, and how they process information from their senses. The word 'spectrum' means autism shows up differently in each person: some need daily support, while others live completely independently.

According to the World Health Organization, roughly 1 in 127 children worldwide has autism spectrum disorder. It is diagnosed more often in boys than in girls, although in girls the condition is often recognised later or with different signs.

sections.title: Causes
paragraphs: Autism does not have one single cause. Research shows that genetics plays the main role, alongside other factors that affect early brain development before birth.
Autism is not caused by parenting style, and large-scale scientific studies have clearly shown that vaccines do not cause autism.
Autism can occur on its own or together with other conditions, including some rare genetic diseases such as fragile X syndrome, Phelan-McDermid syndrome and other rare disorders.

sections.title: Early signs
paragraphs: Signs usually appear in the first two to three years of life. Parents may notice that the child:
list: rarely makes eye contact or responds to their name
does not point, wave or share interest with others
starts talking late or loses words and skills they had before
repeats movements, sounds or phrases
strongly prefers routine and is upset by changes
is overly sensitive — or, on the contrary, less sensitive — to sounds, light, textures or pain
has strong interests focused on a particular topic
sections.after: One sign on its own does not mean a child has autism spectrum disorder. If you are concerned, consult your paediatrician — early assessment is always better than waiting.

sections.title: Diagnosis
paragraphs: There is no blood test for autism. It is diagnosed by specialists — such as a child neurologist, child psychiatrist or developmental psychologist — who observe the child’s behaviour and development and talk with the family.
Screening questionnaires such as the M-CHAT can be used at routine check-ups between 18 and 24 months. Autism can be reliably diagnosed from around the age of two.

sections.title: Support and therapy
paragraphs: Every child on the autism spectrum is different, so support should be planned around their individual strengths and needs. Early intervention matters a great deal. Commonly used approaches include:
list: Speech and language therapy, including alternative communication (AAC)
Occupational therapy and sensory support
Behavioural and developmental therapies
Special education and inclusive school support
Parent training and family support
Medical management of co-occurring conditions, such as sleep disorders or epilepsy

sections.title: Living with autism
paragraphs: With understanding, acceptance and the right support, children on the autism spectrum grow, learn and build fulfilling lives. An inclusive society — at school, in clinics and in everyday life — is one of the most powerful forms of support.

rare.title: Rare diseases
rare.lead: A disease is called rare when it affects fewer than 1 in 2,000 people. Today, between 6,000 and 8,000 rare diseases are known, and about 70% of them begin in childhood.

items.name: PMM2-CDG
items.text: The most common type of CDG, caused by changes in the PMM2 gene. It often causes low muscle tone, crossed eyes, balance problems and developmental delay, and can affect the liver, heart and blood clotting.

items.name: MPI-CDG
items.text: A type of CDG that mainly affects the liver and gut, causing diarrhoea, low blood sugar and clotting problems. Unlike most CDG types, it can be treated with oral mannose — which is why early diagnosis matters.

items.name: Rett syndrome
items.text: A genetic condition, usually caused by changes in the MECP2 gene, that mostly affects girls. After a period of typical development, children lose purposeful hand use and speech, and develop repetitive hand movements.

items.name: Angelman syndrome
items.text: Caused by loss of function of the UBE3A gene on chromosome 15. Children have severe speech delay, balance problems, seizures, and often a very happy, excitable personality.

items.name: Phelan-McDermid syndrome
items.text: Caused by a deletion at the end of chromosome 22 (22q13) or changes in the SHANK3 gene. It causes low muscle tone, delayed or absent speech and developmental delay, and is often associated with autism.

items.name: Fragile X syndrome
items.text: The most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, caused by changes in the FMR1 gene. It can cause learning difficulties, anxiety and hyperactivity, and many affected children are also autistic.

about.lead: The Foundation for CDG Syndrome and Autism was created by parents who know from their own experience how hard the road to a rare diagnosis can be.

items.text: On 16 May, families, doctors and researchers around the world raise awareness of congenital disorders of glycosylation. It is a day to share stories, support research and help more children get an early diagnosis.

beneficiary.title: Apply for support
beneficiary.lead: Does your child have CDG syndrome, autism or another rare disease? Fill in the application form and our team will contact you. If your child has CDG syndrome, autism spectrum disorder or another rare disease that requires ongoing therapeutic support, you can apply to the foundation.
who: Parents or legal guardians of children with CDG syndrome, autism spectrum disorder or another rare disease.
Families who need help covering costs that the state or insurance does not pay, or only partly covers.
Parents or legal guardians of children who already have a confirmed diagnosis.

steps.title: Fill in the form
steps.text: Provide information about the child, the parent or guardian, the family’s finances and the child’s medical condition.

steps.title: Describe the need
steps.text: Tell us what support you need — therapy, consultation, treatment, medication or equipment — and the amount requested.

steps.title: Attach documents
steps.text: Prepare medical documents, the child’s photos and other supporting files.

steps.title: Review and contact
steps.text: Our team reviews each application carefully and contacts the family about next steps.

docs: Medical documentation confirming the diagnosis — the official conclusion of the treating doctor or institution / form No. 100, genetic test results (if available) and studies carried out in the last 6 months.
An invoice for the therapy cost to be reimbursed.
The child's birth certificate and an identity document of the parent or legal guardian.
Photos of the child (with or without consent for their use).
Documents confirming other assistance the family has already received (if any).
